AlberdiLab | hilldiv3 manuscript Microflora Danica worked example: data and diversity Alberdi Lab Last update: 2026-10-09 Chapter 1 Introduction This webbook contains the data and reproducible code for the Microflora Danica worked example in the hilldiv3 manuscript. The selected panel contains sample and genome metadata, a representative MAG abundance matrix, and a phylogenetic tree. The chapters describe the panel and begin neutral and phylogenetic diversity analyses. 1.1 Prepare the R environment 1.1.1 Environment Clone the GitHub repository and open hilldiv3-ms.Rproj, or create a new RStudio project from: https://github.com/alberdilab/hilldiv3-ms.git 1.1.2 Libraries The book uses these R packages: library(data.table) library(ape) library(knitr) library(ggplot2) library(maps) library(hilldiv3) stopifnot(utils::packageVersion("hilldiv3") >= "3.1.0.9000") 1.2 Analysis steps 1.2.1 Step 0 - Data preparation The data preparation chapter describes the committed Microflora Danica panel, loads it, and checks its sample, genome, abundance, and tree alignment. The source-download and preparation scripts are in scripts/. 1.2.2 Step 1 - Data overview The data overview chapter summarizes sample coverage, sampling dates, geography, and representative genomes. 1.2.3 Step 2 - Initial diversity analyses The diversity analyses chapter calculates neutral and phylogenetic Hill numbers at orders 0, 1, and 2, traces diversity profiles across orders, then partitions diversity within and between the eight habitat classes. The hilldiv3 calls appear in highlighted code blocks. 1.2.4 Step 3 - Pairwise beta diversity The pairwise beta diversity chapter compares every pair of samples with neutral and phylogenetic Hill-number C dissimilarity. It summarizes within- and between-habitat pairs and shows habitat heatmaps and sample-level ordinations at \(q=0\) and \(q=1\). The hillpair() calls are shown before the code that formats their results. 1.2.5 Step 4 - Taxonomic shares and contributions The taxonomic shares chapter uses hillshare() to allocate neutral and phylogenetic Hill power sums to four named phyla and the remaining representatives. A focused agricultural field versus natural grassland soil comparison shows how a nearly stable Actinomycetota share conceals opposing Gaiellales and Streptosporangiales patterns. hillcontrib() then attributes the same neutral and phylogenetic dissimilarities to the phyla and these orders.

Chapter 2 Data preparation 2.1 Input data 2.2 Load the staged panel 2.3 Check the staged objects 2.4 Sources 2.5 Rebuild and verify

Chapter 2 Data preparation The staged panel contains 360 geographically dispersed Microflora Danica samples: 45 from each of eight habitat classes. It uses the same locked sample and representative genome selections as the gifter case study. 2.1 Input data File Contents data/mag_relative_abundance.tsv.xz Relative abundances for 5,518 representative MAGs (rows) and 360 samples (columns). The first column is genome_id. data/sample_metadata.tsv Sample metadata in abundance-column order, including habitat class, ontology, location, date, and selection audit. data/representative_metadata.tsv Metadata for the 95% ANI species representatives in abundance-row order. data/representative_tree.nwk Source tree pruned to the 5,518 representative genome_id tips, retaining source branch lengths. 2.2 Load the staged panel The committed tables and tree are the inputs to the following chapters. Load them from the repository root: sample_metadata <- data.table::fread( "data/sample_metadata.tsv", data.table = FALSE ) genome_metadata <- data.table::fread( "data/representative_metadata.tsv", data.table = FALSE ) genome_abundance <- data.table::fread( cmd = "xz -dc data/mag_relative_abundance.tsv.xz", data.table = FALSE, check.names = FALSE ) genome_tree <- ape::read.tree("data/representative_tree.nwk") The selected panel has 45 samples in each habitat class: habitats <- table(sample_metadata$habitat_label) knitr::kable( data.frame(habitat = names(habitats), samples = as.integer(habitats)), col.names = c("Habitat", "Samples") ) Habitat Samples Agricultural field soil 45 Natural bog/fen soil 45 Natural forest soil 45 Natural freshwater sediment 45 Natural grassland soil 45 Natural saltwater sediment 45 Urban greenspace soil 45 Urban wastewater water 45 2.3 Check the staged objects The abundance rows and columns must align with the metadata, and the tree must contain exactly the representative genomes: stopifnot( nrow(sample_metadata) == 360L, nrow(genome_metadata) == 5518L, nrow(genome_abundance) == 5518L, ncol(genome_abundance) == 361L, length(habitats) == 8L, all(habitats == 45L), identical(genome_abundance$genome_id, genome_metadata$genome_id), identical(names(genome_abundance)[-1L], sample_metadata$sample_id), setequal(genome_tree$tip.label, genome_metadata$genome_id) ) profile_totals <- colSums(as.matrix(genome_abundance[-1L])) stopifnot(all(is.finite(profile_totals)), all(profile_totals > 0.99 & profile_totals < 1.01)) cat(sprintf( "%d samples, %d representative genomes, %d tree tips; profile sums %.6f–%.6f.\n", nrow(sample_metadata), nrow(genome_metadata), ape::Ntip(genome_tree), min(profile_totals), max(profile_totals) )) 360 samples, 5518 representative genomes, 5518 tree tips; profile sums 0.999988–1.000015. The abundance values are proportions of the published MFD MAG profile, not genome or read counts. The preparation script keeps strain (t__) rows from the Sylph profiles, maps MAGs to their published secondary_cluster, sums each 95% ANI cluster, and divides percentages by 100. It assigns each cluster profile to the deposited representative MAG. It does not renormalize profiles. The representative abundance therefore stands for its cluster; it does not imply that all members have identical gene content. These values describe the MFD MAG profile, not the fraction of all DNA in each sample. 2.4 Sources The primary study is Singleton and colleagues, The Microflora Danica atlas of Danish environmental microbiomes. The Microflora Danica data deposit provides Nitrifiers.tar.gz, including the published MAG metadata and Sylph abundance table. Please cite both the study and deposit when using these data, and consult the deposit for its reuse terms. The sample and representative tables are copies of the locked panels at gifter commit f04f7de. The source tree is gtdb-shallow.tree from the MFD companion repository at commit 957591d. Tips outside the representative panel were removed. 2.5 Rebuild and verify The committed files are ready to use. To rebuild them from the pinned public sources, install R packages data.table and ape, then run: bash scripts/fetch-source-data.sh Rscript scripts/prepare-data.R Rscript scripts/check-data.R The source archive is about 228 MB. Downloads remain in the ignored sources/ directory. The preparation script also accepts paths to existing MAG metadata, abundance TSV.xz, and source tree files, in that order. To verify the committed snapshot byte for byte: shasum -a 256 -c data/SHA256SUMS The checker verifies sample and genome IDs, 45 samples per habitat, table ordering, finite nonnegative abundances, near-unit profile sums, and exact tree-tip identity. In this snapshot, sample profile totals range from 0.999988 to 1.000015.

Chapter 4 Initial diversity analyses 4.1 Within-sample diversity 4.2 Diversity profiles across orders 4.3 Partitioning across habitats

Chapter 4 Initial diversity analyses We use hilldiv3 to describe diversity in the selected panel. Neutral Hill numbers use representative relative abundances; phylogenetic Hill numbers also use the pruned representative tree. We evaluate diversity orders \(q=0\) (all detected units receive full weight), \(q=1\) (abundance-weighted diversity), and \(q=2\) (common units weighted more strongly). For neutral diversity, \(q=0\) is the count of detected representatives. Functional diversity awaits a matched trait or gene-function table. 4.1 Within-sample diversity hilldiv() calculates one diversity type per call. The tree and pooled reference depth are supplied only for phylogenetic diversity. alpha_neutral <- hilldiv3::hilldiv( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), type = "neutral" ) alpha_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hilldiv( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), tree = genome_tree, type = "phylogenetic", reference = "pool" ) For the plots and table below, the results are joined to habitat labels. ggplot2::ggplot(alpha_diversity, ggplot2::aes(x = value, y = habitat)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.55, fill = "#e6c7c7", colour = "#702626") + ggplot2::geom_jitter(height = 0.13, width = 0, alpha = 0.28, size = 0.65, colour = "#702626") + ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(type, order), ncol = 3, scales = "free_x") + ggplot2::labs(x = "Hill diversity", y = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Hill numbers for 45 samples in each habitat class. Boxes show medians and interquartile ranges; points are individual samples. Horizontal scales differ by panel. q1 <- alpha_diversity[alpha_diversity$q == 1, ] q1_summary <- aggregate( value ~ habitat + type, data = q1, FUN = function(x) sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]", median(x), unname(quantile(x, 0.25)), unname(quantile(x, 0.75))) ) q1_neutral <- q1_summary[q1_summary$type == "Neutral", c("habitat", "value")] q1_phylo <- q1_summary[q1_summary$type == "Phylogenetic", c("habitat", "value")] names(q1_neutral)[2] <- "Neutral q = 1" names(q1_phylo)[2] <- "Phylogenetic q = 1" q1_table <- merge(q1_neutral, q1_phylo, by = "habitat", sort = FALSE) q1_table <- q1_table[match(habitat_levels, q1_table$habitat), ] names(q1_table)[1] <- "Habitat" rownames(q1_table) <- NULL knitr::kable(q1_table, row.names = FALSE) Habitat Neutral q = 1 Phylogenetic q = 1 Agricultural field soil 47.8 [41.2–58.8] 4.9 [4.5–5.1] Natural grassland soil 55.1 [38.9–67.3] 4.5 [4.1–5.0] Natural forest soil 74.5 [47.9–107.0] 4.8 [4.3–5.3] Urban greenspace soil 48.4 [39.1–64.9] 4.8 [4.4–5.1] Natural bog/fen soil 52.7 [35.6–67.6] 4.4 [3.8–5.1] Natural freshwater sediment 50.6 [32.8–73.2] 5.4 [4.3–6.2] Natural saltwater sediment 48.3 [37.4–65.7] 4.7 [3.9–5.1] Urban wastewater water 78.0 [66.6–93.6] 7.9 [7.3–8.5] Median [interquartile range] of \(q=1\) diversity by habitat. At \(q=1\), median neutral diversity ranges from 47.8 in Agricultural field soil to 78.0 in Urban wastewater water. The phylogenetic values use hilldiv3’s common pooled reference tree depth, so samples are evaluated on the same scale. Their numerical values should be compared within the phylogenetic panels, rather than interpreted as counts of MAGs. Neutral \(q=0\) is the number of representatives with a positive reported abundance; it is sensitive to very small values in the source profiles. 4.2 Diversity profiles across orders hillprof() extends the three selected orders to a finer sweep. To keep the comparison readable, each habitat profile below is the mean of its 45 sample abundance vectors. These are descriptive pooled profiles; their \(q=0\) values count representatives detected in any of those samples. profile_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillprof( habitat_profiles, q = seq(0, 2, by = 0.25), type = "neutral" ) profile_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hillprof( habitat_profiles, q = seq(0, 2, by = 0.25), tree = genome_tree, type = "phylogenetic", reference = "pool" ) ggplot2::ggplot(profiles, ggplot2::aes(x = q, y = value, colour = sample)) + ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = grDevices::hcl.colors( length(habitat_levels), palette = "Dark 3")) + ggplot2::scale_y_log10() + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ type, scales = "free_y") + ggplot2::labs(x = "Diversity order (q)", y = "Hill diversity (log scale)", colour = "Habitat") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Diversity profiles of the mean abundance vector in each habitat. The two panels use separate vertical scales; values should be compared within a panel. The neutral ranking changes with order: bog/fen soil has the highest pooled richness at \(q=0\), while forest soil has the highest diversity at \(q=1\) and \(q=2\). This illustrates why a single diversity order does not capture every aspect of a profile. 4.3 Partitioning across habitats The next calculation partitions diversity across individual samples, habitat classes, and the complete panel. At each step, hilldiv3 reports a beta factor: the effective number of distinct units added at that scale. The two beta factors multiply to give the total gamma-to-alpha ratio. Each sample has equal weight; the design has 45 samples in every habitat class. hillpart() uses the habitat metadata to partition diversity across the sample-to-habitat and habitat-to-panel scales. partition_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillpart( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), hierarchy = ~ habitat_class, metadata = habitat_metadata, type = "neutral" ) partition_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hillpart( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), tree = genome_tree, hierarchy = ~ habitat_class, metadata = habitat_metadata, type = "phylogenetic" ) partition_neutral <- plain_hill_result(partition_neutral) partition_phylogenetic <- plain_hill_result(partition_phylogenetic) partition_neutral$type <- "Neutral" partition_phylogenetic$type <- "Phylogenetic" partition <- rbind(partition_neutral, partition_phylogenetic) stopifnot(all(is.finite(partition$diversity)), all(is.finite(partition$beta[partition$scale != "sample"]))) within <- partition[partition$scale == "habitat_class", c("type", "q", "beta")] between <- partition[partition$scale == "total", c("type", "q", "beta", "diversity")] names(within)[3] <- "Within habitats" names(between)[3:4] <- c("Between habitats", "Gamma diversity") partition_table <- merge(within, between, by = c("type", "q"), sort = FALSE) partition_table <- partition_table[order(match(partition_table$type, c("Neutral", "Phylogenetic")), partition_table$q), ] knitr::kable(partition_table, digits = 2) type q Within habitats Between habitats Gamma diversity Neutral 0 7.50 3.66 3552.00 Neutral 1 5.04 3.33 893.78 Neutral 2 4.80 2.76 334.78 Phylogenetic 0 4.17 3.29 611.03 Phylogenetic 1 1.46 1.56 21.51 Phylogenetic 2 1.12 1.12 6.19 Hierarchical Hill-number partition. Beta factors describe sample-to-habitat and habitat-to-panel turnover; gamma is diversity in the full panel. At \(q=1\), neutral beta diversity is 5.04 from samples to habitats and 3.33 from habitats to the full panel. The corresponding phylogenetic factors are 1.46 and 1.56. These are descriptive comparisons of a geographically selected panel. Habitat and collection year are not independently balanced, so these summaries do not by themselves establish habitat effects. Relative abundances also cannot support read-count rarefaction or sampling-depth uncertainty estimates.

Chapter 5 Pairwise beta diversity 5.1 Within and between habitats 5.2 Habitat pair comparisons 5.3 Sample-level ordination

Chapter 5 Pairwise beta diversity The diversity chapter partitions turnover across the whole panel. Here we compare every pair of the 360 samples with hilldiv3::hillpair(). For each pair, we use the C dissimilarity, the complement of the C overlap derived from multiplicative Hill beta diversity. It ranges from zero for identical communities to one for no overlap. We calculate neutral and phylogenetic values at \(q=0\), \(q=1\), and \(q=2\) using the same representative profiles and tree as above. Each type and order has 6.462^{4} unique sample pairs. The two hillpair() calls return one row per sample pair and order. We request the long-format result so the sample IDs can be joined to their habitats. pair_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillpair( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), metric = "C", type = "neutral", out = "tibble" ) pair_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hillpair( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), metric = "C", tree = genome_tree, type = "phylogenetic", out = "tibble" ) 5.1 Within and between habitats The table summarizes all sample pairs in each category. A habitat contributes 990 within-habitat pairs; two distinct habitats contribute 2,025 pairs. These pairs share samples, so their values are descriptive observations rather than independent replicates for a significance test. pair_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply( split(pairwise, list(pairwise$type, pairwise$q, pairwise$comparison), drop = TRUE), function(d) data.frame( Type = as.character(d$type[1]), q = d$q[1], Comparison = d$comparison[1], Pairs = nrow(d), Median = median(d$value), Q1 = unname(quantile(d$value, 0.25)), Q3 = unname(quantile(d$value, 0.75)) ) )) pair_summary <- pair_summary[ order(match(pair_summary$Type, c("Neutral", "Phylogenetic")), pair_summary$q, match(pair_summary$Comparison, c("Within habitat", "Between habitats"))), ] pair_summary$`Median [IQR]` <- sprintf( "%.3f [%.3f–%.3f]", pair_summary$Median, pair_summary$Q1, pair_summary$Q3 ) knitr::kable(pair_summary[c("Type", "q", "Comparison", "Pairs", "Median [IQR]")], row.names = FALSE) Type q Comparison Pairs Median [IQR] Neutral 0 Within habitat 7920 0.714 [0.484–0.898] Neutral 0 Between habitats 56700 0.992 [0.872–1.000] Neutral 1 Within habitat 7920 0.748 [0.527–0.923] Neutral 1 Between habitats 56700 0.999 [0.902–1.000] Neutral 2 Within habitat 7920 0.842 [0.639–0.971] Neutral 2 Between habitats 56700 1.000 [0.950–1.000] Phylogenetic 0 Within habitat 7920 0.438 [0.297–0.576] Phylogenetic 0 Between habitats 56700 0.758 [0.570–0.843] Phylogenetic 1 Within habitat 7920 0.183 [0.115–0.285] Phylogenetic 1 Between habitats 56700 0.454 [0.258–0.545] Phylogenetic 2 Within habitat 7920 0.085 [0.043–0.155] Phylogenetic 2 Between habitats 56700 0.217 [0.124–0.300] C dissimilarity for all unique sample pairs, summarized as median [interquartile range]. Each within-habitat row contains eight sets of 990 pairs; each between-habitat row contains 28 sets of 2,025 pairs. At \(q=1\), neutral C dissimilarity has median 0.748 within habitats and 0.999 between habitats. At \(q=1\), phylogenetic C dissimilarity has median 0.183 within habitats and 0.454 between habitats. Neutral between-habitat medians are close to one at every order, including \(q=2\), where common representatives carry the most weight. Phylogenetic between-habitat medians decrease from \(q=0\) to \(q=2\), consistent with greater shared branch structure among the more abundant representatives. 5.2 Habitat pair comparisons We take the median across the sample pairs for each pair of habitats. A diagonal cell summarizes pairs of different samples from the same habitat; it is not a self-comparison. The heatmaps show \(q=1\), with a common zero-to-one colour scale for both diversity types. ggplot2::ggplot(heatmap_data, ggplot2::aes(x = Habitat2, y = Habitat1, fill = median)) + ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) + ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", median), colour = median > 0.55), size = 3) + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#292929", `TRUE` = "white"), guide = "none") + ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7f7f7", high = "#8b1e1e", limits = c(0, 1), name = "C dissimilarity") + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ type, ncol = 1) + ggplot2::coord_equal() + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(), axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Median \(q=1\) C dissimilarity across 990 pairs on each diagonal and 2,025 pairs in each off-diagonal habitat combination. The matrices are symmetric. Saltwater sediment and wastewater are nearly maximally dissimilar to the soil habitats at \(q=1\) in the neutral analysis. Their phylogenetic dissimilarities are lower, showing that the sample pairs retain some shared evolutionary branch structure despite little overlap in representative profiles. 5.3 Sample-level ordination Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) projects the \(q=0\) and \(q=1\) dissimilarities into two dimensions. At \(q=0\), neutral dissimilarity reflects overlap among detected representatives; phylogenetic dissimilarity also accounts for their shared tree branches. We apply a Cailliez correction because C dissimilarity need not be Euclidean. Axis percentages refer to the corrected distance matrix in each panel. ggplot2::ggplot(ordination, ggplot2::aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2, colour = habitat)) + ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 1.3) + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = grDevices::hcl.colors( length(habitat_levels), palette = "Dark 3")) + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 2, scales = "free") + ggplot2::labs(x = "PCoA 1", y = "PCoA 2", colour = "Habitat") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Each point is one sample. The top row shows richness-based \(q=0\) dissimilarity; the bottom row shows abundance-weighted \(q=1\) dissimilarity. Axis percentages are the shares of positive eigenvalues after the Cailliez correction; coordinates are comparable only within a panel. The pairwise patterns describe this selected panel. Pairs sharing samples are dependent, and habitat class is partly confounded with sampling year. We do not treat visual separation or differences between pairwise medians as a formal test of a habitat effect. As elsewhere, \(q=0\) responds to very small reported abundances in the source profiles.

Chapter 6 Taxonomic shares and dissimilarity contributions 6.1 Define the genome sets 6.2 Shares across habitats 6.3 A stable phylum total hides order turnover 6.4 A contrasting phylum-level signal 6.5 How order and tree weighting change a share 6.6 Which phyla account for dissimilarity?

Chapter 6 Taxonomic shares and dissimilarity contributions The diversity and pairwise beta diversity chapters describe whole communities. Here we use hilldiv3::hillshare() to allocate each sample’s Hill power sum to sets of representative MAGs. A share is a fraction between zero and one, not a fraction of the effective Hill number reported by hilldiv(). The calculation is descriptive; it does not test whether a phylum is enriched in a habitat. This chapter was rendered with hilldiv3 version 3.1.0.9000. 6.1 Define the genome sets We use four phyla that have substantial abundance or dissimilarity contributions in the field–grassland soil comparison. The Other set contains every remaining representative, so the five sets are disjoint and exhaustive. Each representative stands for its published 95% ANI cluster; the shares describe those cluster profiles, not the abundance of every MAG within a cluster. phylum <- sub("^p__", "", genome_metadata$phylum) focus_phyla <- c("Pseudomonadota", "Actinomycetota", "Acidobacteriota", "Thermoproteota") contrast_habitats <- c("Agricultural field soil", "Natural grassland soil") share_sets <- lapply(focus_phyla, function(name) { genome_metadata$genome_id[phylum == name] }) names(share_sets) <- focus_phyla share_sets$Other <- genome_metadata$genome_id[!phylum %in% focus_phyla] stopifnot(sum(lengths(share_sets)) == nrow(genome_metadata), setequal(unlist(share_sets, use.names = FALSE), genome_metadata$genome_id)) hillshare() returns one row for each sample, order, diversity type, and set. The phylogenetic call uses the same representative tree as the earlier chapters. Both diversity types are requested together. shares <- hilldiv3::hillshare( overview_abundance, q = c(0, 1, 2), tree = genome_tree, type = c("neutral", "phylogenetic"), sets = share_sets ) 6.2 Shares across habitats The heatmap shows the median share among the 45 samples in each habitat. Its colour scale is the same in every panel. At neutral \(q=1\), a set’s share equals its summed relative abundance. At \(q=0\), each detected representative has equal neutral weight; at \(q=2\), abundant representatives carry more weight. Phylogenetic shares also allocate the weights of tree branches to their descendant representatives. ggplot2::ggplot(share_medians, ggplot2::aes(x = Habitat, y = Set, fill = share)) + ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) + ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient( low = "#f7f7f7", high = "#8b1e1e", limits = c(0, 1), labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x), name = "Median share" ) + ggplot2::facet_grid(Order ~ Type) + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + ggplot2::theme( panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(), axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold") ) Median power-sum shares in each habitat. Medians are taken separately for each set, so the displayed medians need not sum to one; the five shares sum to one within every individual sample, type, and order. 6.3 A stable phylum total hides order turnover The broad habitat comparison in the Microflora Danica atlas places fields and grasslands among similar soil environments. Its supplementary genome analysis notes widespread Gaiella and a Trebonia species found in grasslands. We use the representative MAG profiles to ask whether similar abundance at the phylum level can conceal opposing changes among its members. For Actinomycetota, we define separate sets for Gaiellales and Streptosporangiales. These sets are disjoint; Other completes the partition. The parent phylum’s share comes from the earlier hillshare() result. At neutral \(q=1\), each share equals that set’s summed abundance within the MFD MAG profile. The order names are taxonomic assignments, not functional annotations. actino_order_shares <- hilldiv3::hillshare( overview_abundance[, soil_samples, drop = FALSE], q = 1, type = "neutral", sets = actino_order_sets ) ggplot2::ggplot(actino_plot_data, ggplot2::aes(x = Habitat, y = share, fill = Habitat)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.52, alpha = 0.55) + ggplot2::geom_point( position = ggplot2::position_jitter(width = 0.13, height = 0, seed = 42), size = 0.9, alpha = 0.4 ) + ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c("Field soil" = "#a52929", "Grassland soil" = "#1b6b75")) + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous( labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.07)) ) + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ Taxon, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Neutral share (q = 1)") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + ggplot2::theme( legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold") ) Each point is one sample; boxes show medians and interquartile ranges. The percentage scale differs between taxon panels. Shares are relative to the detected MFD MAG profile, not to all DNA in a sample. The median Actinomycetota share is 34.9% in fields and 34.7% in grasslands. Within that nearly stable total, Gaiellales is 12.5% versus 3.0%, while Streptosporangiales is 1.0% versus 5.9%. The order distributions overlap, but their directions also appear when we restrict the panel to the two sampling projects containing both habitats (16 field and 7 grassland samples): the Gaiellales means are 12.3% and 4.1%, and the Streptosporangiales means are 8.7% and 18.3%, respectively. This subset is small and does not establish independence from sampling context. The pattern is a within-phylum compositional contrast, not a claim about the orders’ ecological functions. 6.4 A contrasting phylum-level signal Thermoproteota has a higher \(q=1\) share in field soil than in grassland soil. The next figure shows the sample-level values for both diversity types rather than only the habitat medians in the heatmap. ggplot2::ggplot(thermoproteota, ggplot2::aes(x = share, y = habitat)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.55, fill = "#e6c7c7", colour = "#702626") + ggplot2::geom_jitter(height = 0.13, width = 0, alpha = 0.4, size = 0.8, colour = "#702626") + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ Type, nrow = 1) + ggplot2::scale_x_continuous( labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x), breaks = seq(0, 0.4, by = 0.1), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.03)) ) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Thermoproteota share (q = 1)", y = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Each point is one sample; boxes show medians and interquartile ranges. The panels share an abundance scale. A zero means no representative from this phylum was detected in that sample. The median neutral Thermoproteota share is 9.7% in field soil and 1.0% in grassland soil. The distributions overlap, and these unpaired samples do not establish a land-use effect. 6.5 How order and tree weighting change a share For Pseudomonadota, the next plot compares sample medians and interquartile ranges across orders in four soil habitats. The lines connect summaries, not individual samples. A shared vertical scale makes both diversity types directly visible. ggplot2::ggplot(share_order, ggplot2::aes(x = q, y = median, colour = Type, group = Type)) + ggplot2::geom_errorbar(ggplot2::aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.09, linewidth = 0.5) + ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) + ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1, 2)) + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous( limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2), labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x) ) + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c("Neutral" = "#702626", "Phylogenetic" = "#1b6b75")) + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ habitat, ncol = 2) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Diversity order (q)", y = "Pseudomonadota share", colour = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold")) Points are medians across 45 samples; bars are interquartile ranges. They describe the selected panel and are not confidence intervals. The phylogenetic tree is rooted but not ultrametric. At \(q=1\), differences between neutral and phylogenetic shares reflect root-to-tip path lengths in addition to abundance. At other orders, shared branch weights also affect the allocation. The panel has no matched functional-distance matrix, so we restrict this example to neutral and phylogenetic shares. Habitat and sampling year are partly confounded; these figures do not establish a habitat effect. 6.6 Which phyla account for dissimilarity? We compare the mean abundance profiles of agricultural field soil and natural grassland soil, calculated earlier from 45 samples per habitat. Both are soils, but the source metadata classify one as agricultural and the other as natural. This gives the contribution analysis an ecological land-use question with a shared sample matrix. It is one comparison of two habitat mean vectors, not the median of the 2,025 individual sample pairs shown in the pairwise analysis. The samples are not matched on soil properties, vegetation, location, or sampling year, so this descriptive contrast cannot isolate an effect of human land use. The same five disjoint genome sets used for hillshare() cover every representative. Here hillcontrib() attributes the \(q=1\) C dissimilarity to those sets. A contribution is a part of the dissimilarity, whereas the earlier power-sum share describes one profile on its own. contrib_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillcontrib( contrast_profiles, q = 1, metric = "C", type = "neutral", sets = share_sets ) contrib_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hillcontrib( contrast_profiles, q = 1, metric = "C", tree = genome_tree, type = "phylogenetic", sets = share_sets ) ggplot2::ggplot(contributions, ggplot2::aes(x = Type, y = contribution, fill = set)) + ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.55) + ggplot2::coord_flip() + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous( limits = c(0, 0.3), breaks = seq(0, 0.3, by = 0.1), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0)) ) + ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c( Pseudomonadota = "#702626", Actinomycetota = "#ca725c", Acidobacteriota = "#d8b763", Thermoproteota = "#1b6b75", Other = "#a6a6a6" )) + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Contribution to C dissimilarity (q = 1)", fill = "Representative set") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank()) The bar lengths are the C dissimilarities for the same two mean profiles; their segments sum to those values. They are not median contributions among sample pairs. Neutral C dissimilarity is 0.285 and phylogenetic C dissimilarity is 0.048. Actinomycetota accounts for 37.9% of the neutral value and 35.3% of the phylogenetic value. Pseudomonadota and Thermoproteota also make substantial contributions. Phylogenetic attribution allocates shared branch turnover to descendant representatives under hillcontrib()’s specified rule; it is not a unique biological assignment of each branch to a phylum. 6.6.1 The orders behind the Actinomycetota contribution The phylum totals above do not show which Actinomycetota representatives create the difference. We now partition the same two habitat mean profiles into Gaiellales, Streptosporangiales, the remaining Actinomycetota, and all representatives outside the phylum. The four sets are disjoint and exhaustive, so their C contributions sum to the corresponding whole-community values. actino_contrib_neutral <- hilldiv3::hillcontrib( contrast_profiles, q = 1, metric = "C", type = "neutral", sets = actino_contrib_sets ) actino_contrib_phylogenetic <- hilldiv3::hillcontrib( contrast_profiles, q = 1, metric = "C", tree = genome_tree, type = "phylogenetic", sets = actino_contrib_sets ) ggplot2::ggplot(actino_contrib_plot, ggplot2::aes(x = Type, y = Fraction, fill = Set)) + ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.55) + ggplot2::coord_flip() + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous( limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.25), labels = function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0)) ) + ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c( Gaiellales = "#9d2f30", Streptosporangiales = "#d4846e", `Remaining Actinomycetota` = "#a6a6a6" )) + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of Actinomycetota C contribution", fill = "Representative set") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank()) The bars divide the Actinomycetota segment of the preceding figure, not the whole-community C value. Both use the same field and grassland mean profiles; these are not sample-pair medians. Gaiellales and Streptosporangiales together account for 50.2% of Actinomycetota’s neutral contribution and 52.8% of its phylogenetic contribution. Relative to the full C values, these two orders account for 19.1% and 18.6%, respectively. Thus the nearly unchanged phylum abundance does not imply that its constituent representatives are unchanged. The field and grassland samples differ in location, soil properties, sampling project, and year; these descriptive differences cannot be assigned to land management alone. 6.6.2 How phylogenetic weighting redistributes contributions Thermoproteota accounts for 9.1% of the neutral C value and 19.0% of the phylogenetic value. Pseudomonadota moves in the opposite direction, from 32.7% to 22.0% of the phylogenetic value. Representatives assigned to Nitrososphaerales make up 100.0% and 99.7% of Thermoproteota abundance in the field and grassland mean profiles, respectively. That is a taxonomic assignment, not a measurement of function. The contribution shares describe two different C values; no significance test is involved. The figure shows one small clade from each phylum on the same branch-gap colour scale. The nonlinear colour mapping keeps smaller nonzero gaps visible; the legend reports the original gap values. Each panel shows a separate four-MAG clade in the source tree. Horizontal branches are drawn to scale and coloured by the same length-weighted \(q=1\) abundance-gap scale, with nonlinear colour spacing; grey vertical lines connect them. All four Thermoproteota representatives shown are assigned to Nitrososphaerales, and their clade has a larger combined branch gap than the selected Pseudomonadota clade. The shares in the panel headings come from all representatives and branches in each phylum; these selected clades illustrate the contrast but do not alone determine the phylum-wide percentages.
